title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail, and Retail Theft Has Become an Industry
dek: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, and fences clean off the markings and resell, after which the goods go up on secondhand platforms. Goods that can be networked sell for 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant fetch only about a third.
why: High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorised, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation, with plenty of hard numbers.
who: People in retail, consumer goods, supply chain and security compliance, plus investors watching US brick-and-mortar retail margins and the direction of legislation.
skip: The roughly one-minute opening plug for the in-person LA recording can be skipped.

points.h: A third of shrink is self-inflicted
points.body: Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious, which Scott describes as the things we do to ourselves versus the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The figure that has circulated in the industry for years is that of malicious shrink, roughly 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. These percentages move only within a few points each year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been underreported ever since COVID, with neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report fully capturing it.

points.h: Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
points.body: The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal, and these people have one thing on their minds — getting the goods out to exchange for money — so they will get physical, and they have. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and even killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene, just to back off. His attitude is that he is willing to trade shrink for people's safety every single day, and management and the board would back that decision.

points.h: RFID fails the moment it enters a steel store
points.body: Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and yet in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains what's peculiar about Home Depot: it's a hardware store, and the store is full of steel, essentially a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read and only actively transmitting solutions work. He also says tag costs are now almost zero, and the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits is extremely costly. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but to do that for a single drill you have to rework the entire production line, which is very hard to scale.

points.h: Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
points.body: The division of labour works like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, and go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — which might be a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money then goes up to whoever is running the operation, which might be a small crew of just a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works backwards from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

points.h: One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
points.body: Whether to lock up shelves is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there is a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately understand it's a gross margin problem — as long as it breaks even or even makes a little money, locking up is justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and if they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So the categories that get locked up are carefully selected, with a QR code to summon an associate, and the average unlock time is 90 seconds; locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the goods are finally there.

points.h: A fake bill of lading can just drive the goods away
points.body: In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transshipment warehouse and taken elsewhere, even loaded back onto a container ship and shipped away; second, a driver drives eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and moves boxes; third, forging bills of lading and pickup orders, using AI to make the documents look real, and the driver pulls in, says he's there to pick up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new may not be the methods but the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the area that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years; cars sitting in a yard get broken into by a group, and the other side has good intelligence — they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

points.h: AI in security is an efficiency tool
points.body: Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closing and handing over to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They have just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid associates, or appear where they shouldn't. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviours and then recognise the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

points.h: Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
points.body: He says he is very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan co-sponsors, it has passed the House, it is attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he will sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources, and the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination centre. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood then was decriminalisation and defunding the police.

terms.def: Inventory that is on the books but doesn't match up at count, covering both operational errors and theft.
Gang theft for resale profit, spanning multiple stores and even states.
Recruited shoplifters who are given a list, cash or the promise of drugs and go into stores specifically to steal.
The middleman who concentrates stolen goods and strips the markings and price tags before reselling.
Took effect in 2023, requiring online platforms to verify the identity of high-volume sellers, with peer-to-peer sellers excluded.
